paragraphs.text: But it is necessary, brothers, to learn why in ancient times God confined the people to one place and region, and why he did not permit that people to sing the divine songs throughout the whole earth. For this must first be well understood: God does not change, does not alter, and does not shift from one purpose to another. He does not approve one thing at one time and something else at another. Rather, while he himself is unchangeable and unalterable, he adapts himself to human weakness. God speaks, brothers, and often gives laws, not as he is able to, but as we are able to hear. He could have kindled the torch for the nations even through the old song, but those who handled the torch were not strong enough for the proclamation of true religion. For if they themselves received the word of godliness and did not hold fast to it, how could they have handed on the law of godliness to others? Since the people were unsound and faithless, and quickly drawn into the pollutions of the Gentiles, they were confined to one place, so that they at least might be able to practise the law of godliness. Each man among us often does the same. When he has a wife he suspects, he confines her to one place, shuts her up in her chambers, sets eunuchs around her, surrounds her with every kind of guard, and does and contrives everything that protects chastity, since there is no true love there, and no safeguard that comes from a chaste mind, the safeguard that lives alongside a chaste woman. But the man who has a chaste and modest wife does not stop her from going out at all, for in her disposition he has a secure pledge. She goes out to the marketplace, and jealousy is quenched. She meets many men, and the disease of jealousy is nowhere to be found. For the chaste woman has her own character with her as guardian and tutor. What happens among us humans, then, God also does.

A truly beautiful and wonderful hymn the hymnwriter David has struck up for us on the spiritual lyre. With his prophetic tongue he weaves the message of the gospel, and through ancient words he signifies new realities. For what did he cry out? As we have just heard: “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth.” Consider this reverently, beloved, and understand how, by joining the words of the prophets to the words of the gospel, he produces a single harmony of doctrines. We know, brothers, that the new song is set in contrast to the old. But we must inquire what the old song stands for and what the new one stands for. In this way, from the difference between the things themselves, we shall be able to grasp the meaning of the truth. Now the first and most ancient song of all was sung at the Red Sea, when that wonderful man Moses, by divine power, made the sea solid as rock and turned the open sea into land. Striking up a song, he said: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously; horse and rider he has thrown into the sea.” Another old song was sung by the blessed Deborah, when the enemy had been laid low in battle and she raised the victory hymn like some great trophy. You will find yet another old song that arose in the wilderness, when the children of Israel found the well and enjoyed an unexpected grace. Those who read the holy Scriptures genuinely and sincerely can find a great deal said about the old song. It remains for us to inquire what power this new and fresh song has, and what meaning it implies. Pay close attention to me. The old song was confined to one people and limited to one region, that of Palestine, and the people were not permitted to perform the old song outside that region. Since there was one people and one nation, in ancient times both the song and the worship were confined to one place and region. The blessed David also bears witness to this, speaking somewhere in the person of the Jews carried off to Babylon: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” Do you see that the old song was not permitted to spread through all the earth under heaven, but that the hymn was bound up with the nation? But let us take up again what was said by those in Babylon: “Then those who took us captive asked us for words of songs, and those who led us away asked us for a hymn: ‘Sing us one of the songs of Zion.’” Then, bound by the law and forbidden to sing the divine songs in a foreign land, they answer: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” So the old song, as I said before, was expressly confined both to the people and to the region. But the new song spreads through all the earth under heaven and is sung by the whole inhabited world. That is why the prophet, having said “Sing to the Lord a new song,” immediately added: “Sing to the Lord, all the earth.” See how he spreads out the gift, see how he broadens theology, see how he shows the new song in contrast to that old and confined one. And so that no one might blunt its meaning with human conjectures, he did not keep silent about the working of the angelic grace. Having said “Sing to the Lord, all the earth,” he added again: “Proclaim the good news of his salvation from day to day.” What salvation? Clearly he means the much-hymned dispensation of the Savior: that God came among humans out of his love for humankind, that a physician came to dwell among the sick, that the light shone on those in darkness, that the way appeared to those who had gone astray. That way cried out today through the Gospels: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.”

Let no one think that the image set before you is unfitting. For God deals with the people as a husband deals with a wife, not through a union of bodies but through disposition and goodwill. Indeed, the same God, speaking through the prophet to the old synagogue, said plainly: “I betrothed you to myself in judgment and in mercy and in righteousness and in knowledge.” He explained the nature of God’s union. And what is God’s union? Knowledge. For in human union bodies are joined to bodies, but in union with God the soul cleaves to God. As it is said in the one case, “He shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh,” so the soul united to God the Word cries out: “My soul has cleaved to you; your right hand has upheld me.” The old synagogue, then, had the law as its husband, as Isaiah testifies, speaking today through the apostle. For Paul made use of the prophet’s voice, saying: “As it is written, the children of the desolate woman are more than those of her who has a husband.” She, then, had the law as her husband (for I will take up the argument again), but she was under suspicion, since everywhere she betrayed her goodwill toward God by her attachment to idols. For God reproaches her, saying: “You committed adultery with stone and wood, and forgot me, says the Lord.” Since the synagogue’s mind was under suspicion, he rightly confines her to one place and shuts her up in the temple as if in a chamber. He did not even allow an altar to be set up in every place. All Judea and Palestine belonged to the people, but there was only one place that had the altar. That is why Moses too, seeing the wife’s untrustworthiness (for the passage, for the time being, calls the synagogue a wife), knowing the synagogue’s untrustworthiness, proclaimed beforehand: “Take heed to yourself, Israel, that you do not offer your burnt offerings and sacrifices in any place you happen to find, but only in the place which the Lord your God shall choose.” See how she is confined. And rightly so, brothers. Having received an altar in one place, she filled every place with idolatry, as Jeremiah testifies when he cries out: “Your gods were as many as your cities, Judah, and in the streets of Jerusalem you sacrificed to Baal.” If, having been given one place, she filled the whole land with adultery, consider what boundless licentiousness she would have shown if she had been given license everywhere. That is why, brothers, the song was confined to one place, the altar to one place, and that people to one place. But the Church is chaste and modest. She carries Christ about within her everywhere and puts forward countless martyrs as proof of her devotion to her husband, so she is not restricted to any place. Rather, there are altars in every place and teachings in every place. God foretold this through the prophet. Signifying the Church’s abundance and denouncing the ingratitude of the people, he says to them: “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord Almighty, and I will not accept sacrifices from your hands. For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name is glorified among the nations, and in every place a sacrifice is offered to my name, and a pure sacrifice.” See how brilliantly and clearly he has explained the mystical table, the bloodless sacrifice. By pure incense he means the holy prayer that is offered up with the sacrifice. For the incense that gives God rest is not the kind obtained from earthly roots, but the incense sent up from a pure heart: “Let my prayer rise like incense before you.” Do you see how the angelic liturgy is permitted to shine forth everywhere? Do you see how neither the altar nor the song is confined? “In every place incense is offered to my name.” There is, then, a pure sacrifice. First comes the mystical table, the heavenly victim beyond this world. But among us there is also a variety of many sacrifices. Under the old covenant the law had many sacrifices: the sin offering, the one called the burnt offering, the offering of praise, the peace offering, another for lepers being cleansed, and many other different ones for those found in countless defilements. The number of sacrifices under the law was great and beyond measure. But the new grace, when it came, gathered them all into one and established one true sacrifice.

We too have within ourselves other sacrifices, which do not follow the law but befit the angelic grace. Do you wish to learn about these sacrifices that the Church has: how the gift of the gospel is offered up to God without blood or altar or the rest, and how the sacrifice is pure and undefiled? Listen to holy Scripture, which clearly sets this difference and variety before you. The first sacrifice, as I said before, is that spiritual and mystical gift. Paul speaks of it: “Be imitators of God, as beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ also loved us and gave himself up for us to God as an offering and sacrifice, a fragrant aroma.” The second sacrifice is that of the martyrs. And what text bears witness to it? Listen to Paul: “I urge you, brothers, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God.” So you have first the sacrifice of salvation, second that of the martyrs, and third that of prayer: “Let my prayer rise like incense before you, the lifting up of my hands like an evening sacrifice.” Fourth is that of praise, that is, of hymns: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise.” Fifth is that of righteousness: “Then you will delight in a sacrifice of righteousness.” Sixth is that of almsgiving: “A pure and undefiled sacrifice,” it says, “is to visit the poor and orphans in their affliction.” Seventh is that of the victory shout. A victory shout is the triumphant clamor raised in war. For a wail is one thing and a victory shout another: when soldiers shout after a victory in war, that is a victory shout and a signal of victory. That is why the prophet calls blessed those who would come to know Christ’s victory and cry out the hymn against the enemy, saying: “Blessed is the people that knows the victory shout.” A victory shout, then, is the triumphant clamor raised in war. The Savior won the victory over all, saying, “Take courage, I have conquered the world.” So when we send up this hymn to the one who achieved the victory, we fulfil the victory shout that the prophet calls blessed when he says: “I went around and offered in his tabernacle a sacrifice of praise and of shouting.” Eighth, there is another sacrifice to God, a broken spirit: “A broken and humbled heart God will not despise.” Do you see how many sacrifices are practised among us? There is also another new sacrifice, accomplished through the preaching of the gospel, the word of teaching. The apostle Paul speaks of it: “Serving the gospel of God as a priest, so that the offering of God may be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit.” Do you see how he showed that preaching too is offered up to God as a sacrifice? So you have the first sacrifice, the saving gift; the second, that of the martyrs; the third, that of prayer; the fourth, that of the victory shout; the fifth, that of righteousness; the sixth, that of almsgiving; the seventh, that of praise; the eighth, that of compunction and humility; the ninth, that of preaching. Have I left something out? I counted nine, but I thought ten had been handed down. What, then, is the sacrifice I left out? The tenth is that of offering gifts. Paul speaks of it: “I received from Epaphroditus what you sent, an acceptable sacrifice, a fragrant aroma.” Do you see how Paul calls even the gifts offered to the saints a sacrifice? So you have a variety of offerings. “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise.” I have praised all of you, brothers. Or rather, we have all praised you, and God before all of us, for the sacrifice you have displayed, I mean your gifts to the poor. You had mercy on those trampled underfoot in the marketplace, who cried out to God and were heard through you. You imitated God’s love for humankind. You stripped the marketplace of the disgrace of poverty. Almsgiving went out and quenched the shame, for the cry of the poor was a shame to those who have plenty. You have stored up a treasure of life; you have laid up a treasure of righteousness. This is the treasure we must keep before our eyes: the treasure of truth, of righteousness, of love for the poor. For, brothers, there are two treasures: one stored up for evil, and one laid up for good. The treasure of evil is disobedience, unbelief and lawlessness: “Do you not know that God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance? But by your hardness and your impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath, when God’s righteous judgment will be revealed.” Do you see a treasure of sins laid up for the workers of iniquity? See also the treasure from love of the poor, laid up for those who work righteousness. Listen to Paul writing to Timothy: “Charge the rich in this present age not to be haughty, nor to set their hope on the uncertainty of riches, but to do good, to be rich in good works, generous and ready to share, storing up for themselves a good treasure for the future, so that they may take hold of eternal life.” Do you see a treasure of good things? Do you see a treasure of evils? And with whom is the treasure deposited? Clearly with God. He stores up even the treasure of evils for recompense: some he punishes and others he rewards.

Do you want to see how exactly he remembers and how carefully he keeps these treasures? Through Moses he says of those who do evil: “Their vine comes from the vine of Sodom, and their branches from Gomorrah. Their grapes are grapes of gall, their clusters are bitter. Their wine is the rage of dragons, the incurable rage of asps.” And having listed the works of lawlessness, he immediately added: “Are not all these gathered up with me and sealed up in my treasuries? On the day of vengeance I will repay, at the time when their foot slips.” In this way he stores up the treasure of lawlessness for the workers of injustice. But he also stores up the treasures of the kingdom for the workers of righteousness, of which Isaiah says: “Wisdom and knowledge and godliness come from the Lord.” These are treasures of righteousness. Hence the Savior too said to his holy disciples: “Store up for yourselves an unfailing, eternal treasure in heaven.” And he himself, speaking to the rich man, [?]. Let us therefore flee from the treasure of sin and lay up the treasure of almsgiving. It is a good work, able to quench every sin and to undo every transgression. And so that you may learn exactly how much power almsgiving has, consider carefully what I am about to say.

Some sins are directed toward man, others toward God, such as acting impiously, blaspheming, outraging God’s temple, or persecuting or dishonoring God’s Church. All these refer to God. But adultery, theft and wronging others concern our relations with our fellow servants. There is a great difference between sins committed against God and offenses committed against human beings. Nothing, then, is worse than impiety, nothing more wicked than lawlessness toward God, nothing more impious than blasphemy against God. Yet almsgiving can undo even so great a transgression. It cannot do so if one persists in the blasphemy, but it can if one takes back the sin through repentance. Let no one mishear what I say and attack it. My words are addressed not to the folly of fools but to you, the faithful, who have been raised on the truth. Nothing is more terrible than impiety, nothing more wicked than blasphemy. Yet so great an evil is undone through almsgiving, if one comes to the truth sincerely. As proof, take the ancient story of Daniel. Belshazzar, the son of Nebuchadnezzar, once made a drunken mockery of divine things and outraged what was holy. At a common banquet of drunken, impious and blaspheming men, he dared to bring out into their midst the sacred vessels he had taken from Jerusalem and to use them as instruments of drunkenness. “And he brought out,” it says, “the holy vessels of God from Jerusalem, and he drank from them, he and his wives and his concubines and his consorts.” The divine things were outraged not only by being used at a common table but also by debauchery. Yet God is patient even with so great an evil: his forbearing power, his rich grace, his abundant love for humankind awaits our repentance and puts off punishment. God bears with the man who makes a drunken mockery of holy things, and then issues a sentence against him. “For while this was happening,” it says, “there came out upon the plaster of the wall” (that is, upon the coating) “something like the knuckles of a hand, from the wrist to the fingers, the shape of a hand, and it wrote on the wall: Mene, Tekel, Peres.” The words were Hebrew, and the strangeness of the sight [?] astounded the tyrant and his fellow drinkers. They looked for the answer to the riddle, but none could be found. He summoned many interpreters, and they were at a loss before the apparition. Then Daniel is called into their midst. For falsehood must first be at a loss, and then the truth shines out. In the same way, in Egypt the soothsayers and wise men were at a loss, and then Joseph emerged to interpret the truth, and God’s wisdom shone out through his faithful servant. Daniel was called. In came the prophet of holy words, the spiritual book of the Scriptures, the interpreter of the great King. Learn from this the difference between a mere man and a man of God, who is a mere man in nature but immortal in mind. When he entered that banquet of impiety, he was entreated by the master of the feast, I mean the king. For the king said to him: “I know that the holy spirit of God is in you. Interpret this writing for us: what does it mean?” You honor the servant and outrage the master? You revere a man and dishonor God? You acknowledge the Holy Spirit and defile holy things? “I know that the holy spirit of God is in you. For even in my father’s time the spirit was in you abundantly. If, then,” he says, “you solve this question, you will be clothed in purple, with a golden chain around your neck.” But that blessed and wonderful man, counting human gifts as nothing and honoring truth above everything, says: “O king, give your gifts to another man, and give your rewards to others; but I will declare the writing.” Then what is your payment for the interpretation? The reward that comes from God. Or rather, this is my payment for the truth: to interpret the truth itself and to vindicate godliness when it is slandered.

Notice the remarkable thing the righteous man does. He does not interpret the writing first. He first rebukes the king's attitude. And what does he say? "O king, the God of heaven gave the kingdom and power to your father Nebuchadnezzar, and added honor and glory to him." The same goes for you (to be brief). "God gave you the kingdom and the strength, and you forgot God and brought out his silver and gold vessels, and you drank from them, you and your wives and your concubines and your consorts; and you did not bless the one who holds your breath in his hand. Therefore the knuckles of a hand were sent from his presence and wrote his own sentence upon the plaster." And these are the words: "Mene: God has numbered your kingdom and it is complete" (for this is how the Syriac language interprets it, and the Hebrew likewise). "Tekel: God has weighed your kingdom and it has been found wanting. Peres: your kingdom is divided and has been given to the Medes and Persians." At that time the kingdom belonged to the Babylonians alone. And notice the remarkable thing, how he showed that God does all things by number and weight. "He has weighed," he says, "and measured out." Nothing comes from him without measure, nothing without weight, nothing without due order. He brings on judgment by a just measure, and when he punishes he weighs out a punishment in proportion to the sin, not exceeding the sin but matched to it. That is why God, when he once threatened Judah after Samaria had already been destroyed and consumed, says: "I will stretch over Jerusalem the measures of Samaria and the weights of the house of Ephraim." That is: "I will measure out to these the same punishment that I [?] to those." Divine justice is not without measure. It is regulated by measure and rule and weight, as the Savior said in the Gospels: "The measure you measure with will be measured back to you." So God measured and weighed and divided, and the number of the kingdom was complete, he says to the king. And what came after so heavy a sentence? He at once offered a release from the sentence: "And now, O king, let my counsel please you. Redeem your sins by almsgiving and your impiety by compassion for the poor, and perhaps God will be merciful to your transgressions."

Do you see how strong almsgiving is, how much kindness can do, what a work of righteousness mercy toward the poor accomplishes? The prophet gave his counsel so that, if the lawless king had obeyed, grace would have followed instead of a mere promise. Grace was held out, but his heart would not accept correction. That is how powerful kindness toward the poor is. Almsgiving has cleared the spectacle of captives from the marketplace; the spectacle of captivity will be cleared from the whole earth. You saw the marketplace full of captives and you put an end to that distressing sight; God will cut short the punishment brought on for our sins. For God is not unjust, to forget the souls of those unjustly slain or the blood unjustly shed. The saints were slain, but they died for the sake of piety. Do not dwell on the outward appearance of captivity and war. Consider rather that many took up the contest for the sake of chastity and endured death. Many virgins were crowned at a fitting time, as in a time of persecution, and many souls were assailed on their account. And do not think that those whose blood was shed were unworthy of God. This is an ancient pattern in history: God always gives up the saints to dangers, so that through them the power of piety may be displayed. Let no one say: "Well then, if they were holy, would they have been slain? If God cared for them, would they have endured such devastation?" Listen to David, singing of new things through old: "O God, the nations have entered your inheritance, they have defiled the temple." And not simply the temple, but "your holy temple; they have made Jerusalem a watchman's hut in an orchard; they have given the corpses of your servants as food to the birds of heaven, the flesh of your holy ones to the beasts of the earth." If these people now were given up because they were unworthy of piety, how were those of old given up? If some suffer these things now because they are unworthy, how did the saints of the past suffer the same? But if it is the same God who permits all things and arranges them for our good, and who checks the onrush of sin through the saints, then nothing at all that the divine power permits is unjust. God permits these things to train our minds, and the righteous often undergo death on behalf of the unrighteous. The ancient histories give you an old precedent. God pronounces sentence against Adam, saying: "You are earth, and to earth you shall go." Yet the one who received the sentence was still counted among the living, while Abel, who had committed no sin, was slaughtered. The condemned man enjoyed life, and the righteous one was subjected to death. And this was for a good purpose.

God had pronounced against Adam: "On whatever day you eat, you shall surely die." So he did not give death the authority to touch the condemned man first, so that death would not gain a true and secure claim over our race. If death had touched the transgressors first, the punishment would have been irreversible and irrevocable. Instead it came in through injustice, so that it might be banished through righteousness. The righteous were slain, but they were not extinguished, for "the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance." The blood of the righteous was shed, but those who were given up as worthless God calls sons, and avenges as sons. The blessed Moses vouches for my claim that those simply slain by enemies are called sons of God and are avenged as sons. For what does he say in his song? "Rejoice, O nations, with his people, and let all his angels worship him, for the blood of his sons is avenged." If they are sons of God, how were they slain by their adversaries? You see that God allows the righteous to be slain as a test of piety. And I have not forced the text in order to support my view: "Rejoice, O heavens, for the blood of his sons is avenged." They were given up as strangers and are avenged as sons. Being trained in piety is a martyrdom, manifest and acknowledged. Listen to how this is, and consider it, I beg you, and let your mind go deep as you listen. At the tribunal, what else is put before each martyr except the demand to deny God? Having contended against this demand, he receives the acknowledged and undisputed crown of martyrdom. But for the saints who have been slain now, there was no judge passing sentence, only conscience. Many at times transgressed in their minds (I am not condemning anyone, only probing human thoughts). For instance, someone in affliction might have said: "Where is the God I served?" There was a surge and a storm, and the boat was in danger. But suppose someone, tested in those storms, came to his senses again and said: "Is my life confined to this world? Was I waiting for the good things of the earth? Was I not expecting a kingdom? Was I not looking for the resurrection of the dead, for life with the angels, for the life that never grows old? What harm, then, can death do me, when I have eternal goods? I am not troubled by things that pass, for I await the things that are eternal." Whoever put himself to this test in his mind had God as the judge of his mind. He had the reasoning of piety as his advocate, fear as his tribunal, and conscience as his witness, weaving for him the crown of righteousness, and above conscience, God on high awarding the prize to those who labor at piety. For he who sees what is hidden gives his crown openly. "Pray to your Father in secret," he says, "and your Father who is in secret will reward you." So then, is the one who prays in secret crowned, and the one who in secret puts his mind to the test of confession not crowned?

Martyrdom, brothers, is judged not only by the outcome but also by the intention. The martyr does not become a martyr only when he is beheaded. He is a martyr from the moment he shows his intention to confess, even if he does not suffer what a martyr suffers. And who testifies to this? The blessed Paul. He died once, yet he shows that he was dying every day. For what does he say? "I die every day, by the boasting in you that I have in Christ." "I die every day." How do you die, when you are alive? "I died by intention, but I was saved by grace. As far as it depended on men and their designs, and on me, as far as I gave myself up, I die every day. But as far as it depended on divine grace, I was kept safe as a teacher for the Church." For God arranges events for our good. Some he gives up, so that the proven quality of the faithful mind may be displayed; others he preserves, so that he may preserve a leaven for the churches. The virgins were not defiled, for their intention was spotless and their will undefiled. Consider this with me, brother. Virginity receives acknowledged crowns. But which virginity? The virginity of intention, or the virginity of necessity? Do you not know that countless virgins have departed this life with undefiled bodies? Were not many daughters of pagans, of the impure and the impious, snatched away while still waiting for the age of marriage? Were not many young men, their bodies unstained by marriage and union, handed over to death? Young men, I mean, sons of pagans, sons of Jews, sons of impious heretics. Countless people have departed with their bodies virgin. Are crowns for that virginity given at the judgment seat of Christ? Do those multitudes receive the crown of virginity? They do not. If they did receive a crown of virginity, necessity would bear fruit. But since necessity bears no fruit, and every reward belongs to free choice, those countless multitudes remain uncrowned. They had virginity, but they did not have the choice of virginity.

God does not count what is done by necessity, but what is achieved by free choice. If, then, those countless multitudes do not have their virginity counted as virginity, neither do the women defiled against their intention have their defilement counted against them. The body was defiled, but the temple of the soul was not defiled. The body was outraged, but the thoughts were not corrupted. So let no one despair over the great number of saints given up to outrage and captivity. It is often the lot of saints to suffer on behalf of the impious. The Savior, who had committed no sin, is handed over on behalf of sinners. Isaiah cries out: "Man has strayed in his own way, and the Lord handed him over for our sins." And again, the same prophet: "He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth, and the Lord handed him over to our sins, and for the sins of the people he went to death." Do you see? Those who suffer on behalf of the unjust are imitators of Christ. But it also happens otherwise, brothers, if I may widen the account a little. It also happens that some of those slain were guilty of faults. Through a temporary misfortune God released them from their sin; through a blow to the body he healed the wounds of the soul. Death, too, is counted as punishment. And illness is counted as punishment for those among the pious who sin. Who vouches for this? Paul. Nothing should be said without a witness, or on the strength of reasoning alone. When something not in Scripture is said, the mind of the hearers limps: now it nods agreement, now it raises objections; at one moment it rejects the argument as stale, at another it accepts it as plausible. But when the written testimony of the divine voice comes forward, it confirms both the speaker's argument and the hearer's mind. What text, then, will testify for us that the misfortunes and chastisements brought upon people count toward the remission of sins? Listen to the blessed Paul speaking about those who approach the mystical table unworthily: "Do you not know that those who eat unworthily eat and drink judgment on themselves?" And what does he add at once? "That is why many among you are sick." That is why: because they approach the table unworthily. "That is why many are sick, many are weak, and a number have fallen asleep", that is, they are dying, since death too comes upon them in place of their sin. To this he adds at once: "If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged by the Lord." So illness and death are also God's judgment. And what good is that to me after I die? What gain is there after death? "If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged; but when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined, so that we may not be condemned along with the world." God judged it right not to destroy the righteous together with the impious, nor to condemn the holy together with the profane. And very fittingly. It makes no sense for a worshiper of Christ to be punished alongside a blasphemer, or for one who is pious and sings God's praises to be subjected to the same penalty as those who blaspheme and dishonor the truth. That is why God, in hidden and invisible ways and by various means, scourges those among the pious who sin, so that he may present them unblemished at the great judgment seat. He disciplines them here so that he may reckon them their reward there. Take up once more the words of the apostle's thought: "If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged; but when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined, so that we may not be condemned along with the world." The blessed David agrees with this teaching: "Blessed is the man," he says, "whom you discipline, O Lord, and teach from your law, to give him rest from evil days." Whoever is disciplined here will be at rest and will find the divine judgment gentler. And do not be surprised that God sets free in the world to come the pious man who has been disciplined here. You find an even surer pledge of this in divine Scripture. Nothing was worse than the people of Sodom, nothing more impious than those who lived in Gomorrah. Yet because they paid the penalty here, the Savior promises to make their examination gentler: "And you, Capernaum, who were exalted to heaven, will be brought down to Hades. For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Sodom, it would have remained until this day. But it will be more bearable for the land of Sodom and the land of Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for you." If, then, punishment here makes the judgment more bearable even for the people of Sodom, think how those among the pious who are punished here escape the judgment to come. May we all escape it and stand with confidence before the judgment seat of Christ, to whom be glory and power for ever and ever. Amen.
